white_space: Provisional. The WebSearch budget hit 200 of 200 before I could run any of the planned searches. This verdict rests on about 20 direct fetches of named vendor pages plus background knowledge, and several key sites returned 503 or 403 (Aidin, Ensocare, Central Logic, ACEP, GCAL). What I found: no company that uses voice agents to call receiving facilities on a schedule to extract tacit acceptance rules, the name and direct number of the decider, and the hours they answer, then serves that to rural ERs by SMS with a call script. The existing players (OpenBeds, Juvare, ReddiNet, TigerConnect) are registries or referral workflows that depend on facilities entering or updating their own data. The voice-AI companies (Infinitus, Hippocratic, Assort) call for payers, patients and practices, not for facility placement rules. GitHub repository searches returned zero open-source projects. The specific wedges that look unserved are: (1) observed rather than self-reported acceptance rules, including unwritten exclusions such as sitter, autism, weight, out-of-state Medicaid and IV drug history; (2) the identity of the human decider; (3) a nurse-facing SMS workflow with a script for rural critical access hospital charge nurses, who are not the buyers of registry products; (4) a rural-ER buyer that is not the state. Main risks: OpenBeds already sells to state behavioral health authorities in 52 states and territories and could add a 'verified criteria' layer. Facilities may refuse or resent AI intake-line calls. State call-recording and AI-disclosure rules apply. Stale or wrong rules could cause clinical harm and liability. RHTP money flows through state plans, so sales cycles are slow.
evidence_of_demand: Indirect only; nothing found that shows anyone paying for tacit-criteria data specifically. (1) The Rural Health Transformation Program is confirmed at $50B over FY2026-2030 ($10B a year, half split equally among states). Permitted uses include IT infrastructure, technology and AI adoption, and substance use disorder and mental health treatment services, so the funding source is real: https://www.medicaid.gov/resources-for-states/rural-health. The page says nothing about vendor procurement, and I could not verify the claim that every state has posted RHTP funding opportunities. (2) States already pay for behavioral health bed visibility. OpenBeds is claimed in 52 states and territories (https://bamboohealth.com/solutions/openbeds/, redirected from openbeds.net). Juvare announced a California statewide behavioral health bed capacity visibility partnership on Sept 1, 2026 (https://www.juvare.com/thought-leadership/news/juvare-partners-with-california-to-strengthen-statewide-behavioral-health-bed-capacity-visibility/). That shows budget exists and that the registry category is active and well served. (3) Voice AI calling healthcare intake lines is a paid category at scale (https://www.infinitus.ai). Not found or verified: ED boarding statistics, forum complaints, RFPs, and evidence that registries fail on tacit criteria. ACEP returned 403 and no searches were possible. From memory only, unverified: ACEP and other sources report multi-day psychiatric boarding, and some crisis lines such as Georgia's GCAL phone around manually to find beds.
sharper_angle: Do not pitch it as a better bed registry, because OpenBeds and Juvare already sell to states. Sell it as a verified-rules layer: a nightly voice-agent audit of how receiving facilities actually behave, scored against what the registry says, with the named decider and a script. Sequence it in three steps. (1) Start with one rural region and one high-pain vertical, pediatric and adolescent psychiatric placement, where the exclusions are unwritten and ED boarding is worst. Sell to critical access hospital EDs and the state hospital association or rural health office, funded from RHTP behavioral health or IT lines. (2) Ship as SMS and a call-sheet with a 'last verified' timestamp and the name of the person who decides, so it works alongside whatever registry the state uses and is not a rival to it. Start with the founder nurse's binder and use the voice agent to keep it current rather than to build it from nothing. (3) Longer term, offer receiving facilities a listing to pre-qualify referrals, and pitch the data to registry vendors (Bamboo, Juvare) as an accuracy feed or an acquisition target. Before building, validate two things I could not: that a few receiving-unit supervisors will answer an AI or human-assisted call and share their rules on the record, and that the registries do not already capture these criteria. To check the second, request an OpenBeds demo and read a state registry's facility-profile fields. Re-run the competitor search with a fresh web search budget to look for startups in voice-AI placement and transfer calling (post-acute placement vendors such as Aidin, Ensocare and Central Logic, and any new AI transfer-center entrants), because I could not do that here.
